```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Ternant_2017_ck"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-11352-4> (open access)

Ternant et al. described the serum kinetics of three myocardial necrosis
biomarkers -- creatine kinase (CK), cardiac troponin I (cTnI) and the
CK-MB isoenzyme -- after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)
treated by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Each biomarker
was modelled separately (Monolix 4.3.2, SAEM), so the paper contributes three
independent model files:

| Model | Biomarker | Release | Disposition | Baseline production |
|-------|-----------|---------|-------------|---------------------|
| `Ternant_2017_ck` | CK (IU/L) | two transit chains | one compartment | yes (`kin`) |
| `Ternant_2017_ctni` | cTnI (mg/L as printed) | two transit chains | two compartments | no |
| `Ternant_2017_ckmb` | CK-MB (IU/L) | one transit chain | one compartment | yes (`kin`) |

The key output of each model is `BTOT`, the total amount of biomarker
released by the lesion (in concentration units, because the model has no
volume). The authors propose it as a surrogate of infarct size. `BTOT` rises
exponentially with the area at risk (`AAR_PCT`) and is lower in patients
randomized to a cardioprotective conditioning arm (`TRT_CONDITIONING`).

```{r load-models}
mod_ck <- readModelDb("Ternant_2017_ck")
mod_ctni <- readModelDb("Ternant_2017_ctni")
mod_ckmb <- readModelDb("Ternant_2017_ckmb")
```

# Population

`r rxode2::rxode(mod_ck)$population$n_subjects` STEMI patients from three
Lyon conditioning trials (two ischemic postconditioning trials, a cyclosporine
A postconditioning trial and the PCNR postconditioning trial) contributed CK
and cTnI profiles (1965 measurements each; 61 control, 71 conditioned).
`r rxode2::rxode(mod_ckmb)$population$n_subjects` patients from the RIPOST-MI
trial (Angers) contributed CK-MB profiles (735 measurements; 16 control, 17
remote ischemic perconditioning, 16 perconditioning plus local
postconditioning). Median age was 58-59 years and median weight 75-76 kg
(Table 1). Blood was sampled before PCI, every 4 h over the first 24 h and every
6 h over the next 48 h. Each data set was split at random into a learning
subset (2/3) used for estimation and a validation subset (1/3).

Table 1 prints sex as "female/male 101/31" and "40/19"; a STEMI cohort is
predominantly male, so the labels are almost certainly transposed, and the
CK-MB pair sums to 59 rather than 49. The models do not use sex.

The same information is available programmatically via
`rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Ternant_2017_ck"))$population`.

# Model structure

For each patient time zero is the first blood sample (before PCI), and the
biomarker level at that sample, `B0`, is an estimated initial condition. The
rest of the total released amount, `B = BTOT - B0`, enters the central
compartment through a transit release function. With two chains,

    R(t) = B * [Fr * f1(t) + (1 - Fr) * f2(t)]
    f(t) = ktr * (ktr * t)^n * exp(-ktr * t) / Gamma(n + 1)

which is the transit-compartment input of Savic et al. 2007 (paper reference
43) with a non-integer number of transit compartments `n`. The central
compartment follows `dB/dt = R(t) + kprod - ke * B` (Eq. 3) for CK and CK-MB,
and Eqs. 4-5 with peripheral exchange `k12`, `k21` for cTnI. Covariates act on
`BTOT` only: `BTOT = BTOT0 * exp(beta_ARM * ARM + beta_AAR * AAR)`.

# Exact checks

## Elimination half-lives

The Results give elimination half-lives of 11.2 h (CK), 37.8 h (cTnI) and
7.2 h (CK-MB), computed from the kinetic estimates. For CK and CK-MB this is
`log(2) / ke`; for the two-compartment cTnI model it is the terminal
(beta-phase) half-life, which reproduces only with the standard
`dB2/dt = k12 * B1 - k21 * B2` (Eq. 5 prints `+ k21 * B2`).

```{r half-lives}
beta_phase <- function(kel, k12, k21) {
  s <- kel + k12 + k21
  (s - sqrt(s^2 - 4 * kel * k21)) / 2
}
hl <- data.frame(
  biomarker = c("CK", "cTnI", "CK-MB"),
  reported_h = c(11.2, 37.8, 7.2),
  model_h = c(
    log(2) / 0.062,
    log(2) / beta_phase(0.097, 0.11, 0.044),
    log(2) / 0.096
  )
)
hl$pct_diff <- 100 * (hl$model_h - hl$reported_h) / hl$reported_h
knitr::kable(hl, digits = 2)
stopifnot(all(abs(hl$pct_diff) < 1))
```

## Total released amount

The release functions integrate to one, so the area under the
baseline-corrected curve from time zero to infinity is `BTOT / ke` (B0 is
eliminated from the central compartment and B is released into it; for cTnI
all central elimination is through `ke` and the peripheral compartment
returns everything it takes up). This checks the release normalisation, the
`B = BTOT - B0` split and the covariate model in one identity.

```{r auc-identity}
typical_check <- function(mod, out, aar, trt, tmax) {
  mz <- rxode2::zeroRe(rxode2::rxode(mod))
  ev <- data.frame(
    id = 1L, time = seq(0, tmax, by = 0.05), evid = 0L, cmt = "central",
    AAR_PCT = aar, TRT_CONDITIONING = trt
  )
  s <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mz, ev, atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10))
  kin <- if ("kin" %in% names(s)) s$kin else 0
  excess <- s[[out]] - kin / s$kel * (1 - exp(-s$kel * s$time))
  auc <- sum(diff(s$time) * (head(excess, -1) + tail(excess, -1)) / 2)
  data.frame(
    AAR_PCT = aar, TRT_CONDITIONING = trt,
    btot = s$btot[1], auc_excess = auc, expected = s$btot[1] / s$kel[1]
  )
}
idchk <- bind_rows(
  CK = bind_rows(lapply(c(0, 1), \(a) typical_check(mod_ck, "ck", 35, a, 600))),
  cTnI = bind_rows(lapply(c(0, 1), \(a) typical_check(mod_ctni, "troponin_i", 35, a, 1500))),
  `CK-MB` = bind_rows(lapply(c(0, 1), \(a) typical_check(mod_ckmb, "ck_mb", 35, a, 400))),
  .id = "biomarker"
) |>
  mutate(rel_err = (auc_excess - expected) / expected)
knitr::kable(idchk, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 5))
stopifnot(all(abs(idchk$rel_err) < 0.005))
```

The covariate model is exact by construction: the conditioned-to-control
`BTOT` ratio is `exp(beta_ARM)`, i.e. reductions of
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(-0.43)))`% (CK), `r round(100 * (1 - exp(-0.56)))`%
(cTnI) and `r round(100 * (1 - exp(-0.75)))`% (CK-MB).

```{r arm-ratio}
arm_ratio <- idchk |>
  group_by(biomarker) |>
  summarise(ratio = btot[TRT_CONDITIONING == 1] / btot[TRT_CONDITIONING == 0])
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  arm_ratio$ratio[match(c("CK", "cTnI", "CK-MB"), arm_ratio$biomarker)],
  exp(c(-0.43, -0.56, -0.75)),
  tolerance = 1e-8
)))
```

# Virtual cohort

Observed data are not public. The virtual cohort draws the area at risk from
a log-normal distribution matched to the Table 1 median and interquartile
range (redrawing values outside 10-70% ACS, the range seen in Figure 3), and
assigns arms in the trial proportions with at most 200 subjects per arm.
Sampling follows the protocol: before PCI, every 4 h to 24 h, then every 6 h
to 72 h.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(20170906)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20170906)

draw_aar <- function(n, med, q1, q3) {
  sdlog <- (log(q3) - log(q1)) / (2 * qnorm(0.75))
  out <- numeric(0)
  while (length(out) < n) {
    x <- rlnorm(2 * n, log(med), sdlog)
    out <- c(out, x[x >= 10 & x <= 70])
  }
  out[seq_len(n)]
}
obs_times <- c(0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60, 66, 72)

make_cohort <- function(n_ctl, n_trt, med, q1, q3) {
  subj <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n_ctl + n_trt),
    TRT_CONDITIONING = rep(c(0L, 1L), c(n_ctl, n_trt)),
    AAR_PCT = draw_aar(n_ctl + n_trt, med, q1, q3)
  )
  tidyr::crossing(subj, time = obs_times) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L, cmt = "central") |>
    arrange(id, time) |>
    as.data.frame()
}
# CK / cTnI: 61 control vs 71 conditioned; CK-MB: 16 control vs 33 conditioned
cohort_lyon <- make_cohort(172, 200, 34.8, 27.0, 46.5)
cohort_ripost <- make_cohort(97, 200, 37.4, 30.5, 45.7)
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
sim_one <- function(mod, cohort, out, label) {
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(
    mod, cohort,
    keep = c("TRT_CONDITIONING", "AAR_PCT")
  )
  as.data.frame(s) |>
    transmute(
      id, time, TRT_CONDITIONING, AAR_PCT, btot, brel,
      conc = .data[[out]], biomarker = label
    )
}
sim <- bind_rows(
  sim_one(mod_ck, cohort_lyon, "ck", "CK"),
  sim_one(mod_ctni, cohort_lyon, "troponin_i", "cTnI"),
  sim_one(mod_ckmb, cohort_ripost, "ck_mb", "CK-MB")
) |>
  mutate(
    biomarker = factor(biomarker, levels = c("CK", "cTnI", "CK-MB")),
    arm = ifelse(TRT_CONDITIONING == 1, "Conditioned", "Control")
  )
```

Because `BTOT` and `B0` have independent random effects, a few simulated
subjects draw `B0 > BTOT` and therefore a negative post-sampling release
`B = BTOT - B0` (see Assumptions and deviations). The simulated fraction
matches its analytic expectation. These subjects are excluded from the NCA
below, which needs non-negative levels.

```{r negative-release}
# Analytic expectation: log(B0) - log(BTOT) is normal with mean from the
# typical values and covariates and variance omega_B0^2 + omega_BTOT^2.
typ <- data.frame(
  biomarker = c("CK", "cTnI", "CK-MB"),
  b0 = c(173, 0.11, 43.1), btot0 = c(2120, 196, 167),
  e_trt = c(-0.43, -0.56, -0.75), e_aar = c(0.020, 0.019, 0.037),
  om_b0 = c(1.1, 3.7, 1.1), om_btot = c(0.65, 0.80, 0.51)
)
neg_release <- sim |>
  distinct(biomarker, id, brel, TRT_CONDITIONING, AAR_PCT) |>
  mutate(biomarker = as.character(biomarker)) |>
  left_join(typ, by = "biomarker") |>
  mutate(p_neg = pnorm(
    (log(b0) - log(btot0) - e_trt * TRT_CONDITIONING - e_aar * AAR_PCT) /
      sqrt(om_b0^2 + om_btot^2)
  )) |>
  group_by(biomarker) |>
  summarise(
    n_subjects = dplyr::n(),
    pct_negative_B = 100 * mean(brel < 0),
    pct_expected = 100 * mean(p_neg),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
knitr::kable(neg_release, digits = 1)
# A binomial count over about 300 subjects: allow 4 percentage points.
stopifnot(all(abs(neg_release$pct_negative_B - neg_release$pct_expected) < 4))
```

## Prediction intervals (Figure 2)

```{r vpc, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
vpc <- sim |>
  group_by(biomarker, time) |>
  summarise(
    q05 = quantile(conc, 0.05), q50 = median(conc), q95 = quantile(conc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ggplot(vpc, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), fill = "grey75") +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50)) +
  facet_wrap(~biomarker, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time from first blood sample (h)", y = "Biomarker level",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 2 of Ternant 2017 (90% prediction interval and median, both arms pooled)."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r vpc-peaks}
vpc |>
  group_by(biomarker) |>
  summarise(
    `Peak of 95th percentile` = max(q95),
    `Time of peak (h)` = time[which.max(q95)],
    `95th percentile at 72 h` = q95[time == 72],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 0)
```

Read from Figure 2, the upper edge of the published band peaks at about
7500-8000 IU/L (CK), 350 (cTnI) and 700 IU/L (CK-MB), and all three bands
return close to baseline by 72 h. The simulated bands above are on the
protocol sampling grid and exclude residual error, so they are
comparable in order of magnitude only. The CK-MB band in Figure 2 reaches
its maximum within the first 4 h sampling bin, so the figure cannot resolve
the release peak time (see Assumptions and deviations).

## Total released amount by arm (Figure 3)

```{r btot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5}
btot_subj <- sim |> distinct(biomarker, id, arm, AAR_PCT, btot)
btot_subj |>
  group_by(biomarker, arm) |>
  summarise(median_BTOT = median(btot), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = median_BTOT) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 0, caption = "Median simulated BTOT by arm (Figure 3, left).")
ggplot(btot_subj, aes(AAR_PCT, btot, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~biomarker, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Area at risk (% ACS)", y = "BTOT",
    caption = "Compare Figure 3 of Ternant 2017 (right): individual BTOT versus AAR."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r btot-fig3}
fig3_ctl <- data.frame(biomarker = c("CK", "cTnI", "CK-MB"), fig3_control = c(5000, 230, 620))
btot_cmp <- btot_subj |>
  dplyr::filter(arm == "Control") |>
  group_by(biomarker) |>
  summarise(simulated_control = median(btot), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(biomarker = as.character(biomarker)) |>
  left_join(fig3_ctl, by = "biomarker") |>
  mutate(ratio = simulated_control / fig3_control)
knitr::kable(btot_cmp, digits = 2)
```

The Figure 3 values are approximate control-arm medians of the individual
(empirical-Bayes) BTOT estimates in the learning subsets, read from the box
plots. The simulated control-arm medians are within
`r round(min(btot_cmp$ratio), 1)`- to `r round(max(btot_cmp$ratio), 1)`-fold
of them. cTnI shows the largest gap, in line with the population-prediction
bias the authors report for cTnI.

# NCA against Table 1

Table 1 reports the median trapezoidal AUC and peak level of each biomarker
over all patients (both arms pooled). PKNCA is run per biomarker and arm over
the 0-72 h sampling window, and the pooled medians are compared with
Table 1.

```{r pknca}
conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(
  sim |> dplyr::filter(brel >= 0) |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(conc)),
  conc ~ time | biomarker + arm + id
)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 0, end = 72, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, intervals = intervals))
nca_long <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast"))

nca_long |>
  group_by(biomarker, arm, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(median = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = median) |>
  dplyr::rename("Cmax" = cmax, "Tmax (h)" = tmax, "AUC0-72" = auclast) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Median simulated NCA by arm.")
```

```{r nca-compare}
reference <- data.frame(
  biomarker = c("CK", "cTnI", "CK-MB"),
  cmax = c(2745, 97, 306),
  auclast = c(74213, 2607, 5403)
)
simulated <- nca_long |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast")) |>
  select(biomarker, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  mutate(biomarker = as.character(biomarker))
cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated, reference,
  by = "biomarker",
  units = c(cmax = "biomarker units", auclast = "biomarker units*h")
)
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = "Pooled-arm medians: Table 1 (reference) versus simulation.")
```

```{r nca-assert}
pooled <- simulated |>
  group_by(biomarker, PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(sim = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(
    tidyr::pivot_longer(reference, -biomarker, names_to = "PPTESTCD", values_to = "ref"),
    by = c("biomarker", "PPTESTCD")
  ) |>
  mutate(ratio = sim / ref)
# Centre-of-distribution check: a mis-transcribed BTOT, ke or release
# normalisation (for example the unnormalised Eq. 1 as printed, which scales
# the CK release by n / ktr, about 4-fold) moves these medians by
# several-fold.
stopifnot(all(pooled$ratio > 0.5 & pooled$ratio < 2))
```

CK agrees with Table 1 within about 10%, and cTnI within about 20%. The
CK-MB peak is about 30% below Table 1 (flagged), and the CK-MB AUC is about
15% below.
Three things contribute. Table 1 summarises observed levels, which include
residual error, and the maximum of noisy samples is biased upwards. The
virtual cohort is an approximation of the trial. The authors also note a
bias of the population (typical-value) predictions for CK and cTnI that
disappears for individual predictions (Figure 1). For CK-MB, the
conditioned-arm medians of the individual BTOT estimates in Figure 3 (about
400-450 IU/L) lie above the simulated conditioned-arm median. That is, the
population estimate of the arm effect (-0.75 on log BTOT, a 53% reduction)
is larger than the gap between the empirical-Bayes estimates in the figure.
The model AUC (from the population parameters) is compared here with an
observed trapezoidal AUC.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Release function normalisation.** Eq. 1 prints
  `f(t) = (ktr t)^n exp(-ktr t) / Gamma(n)`, which is dimensionless and does
  not integrate to one, so `R(t) = B f(t)` cannot be added to `dB/dt` as
  written. The models use the transit input of the cited reference (Savic
  2007), `ktr (ktr t)^n exp(-ktr t) / Gamma(n + 1)`. With this form, the
  model reproduces the Table 1 AUC medians and the Figure 3 BTOT medians.
  The unnormalised form as printed would multiply the released amount by
  `n / ktr` (for example 3.7 and 3.5 for the two CK chains), several times the
  Table 1 AUC. A shape-`n` gamma density (`ktr (ktr t)^(n - 1) exp(-ktr t) /
  Gamma(n)`) would also integrate to one and give the same AUC, but release
  would peak earlier (by about 2-4 h for cTnI and CK-MB). The maintainers
  compared both forms with Figure 2. For CK-MB, the Savic form matches the
  height of the band peak (about 700 IU/L), where the shape-`n` form
  overshoots it by about 40%. The shape-`n` form declines slightly more like
  the figure between 12 and 30 h. Neither comparison is decisive, so the form
  of the cited reference is used.
* **Eq. 2** prints `R(t) = [F f1(t) + (1 - F) F2(t)]` without the amount `B`;
  the prose ("R(t) = B f(t)" for a single chain) and the definition of `B`
  restore it.
* **Eq. 5 sign.** `dB2/dt = k12 B1 + k21 B2` is printed; the models use
  `- k21 B2`, which is what reproduces the 37.8 h cTnI half-life.
* **B = BTOT - B0.** The Methods define `BTOT = B0 + B`, with `B0` the level
  at the first sample (Table 2 'B1') and `B` the amount released afterwards.
  The models follow this literally. Because `BTOT` and `B0` carry
  independent random effects, a small fraction of simulated subjects (about
  1% for CK, 2% for cTnI and 4% for CK-MB in a cohort like the trials') have
  `B0 > BTOT`.
  These subjects get a negative release term and a profile below their
  starting level. The paper does not say how the authors handled this.
* **B2(0).** Table 2 reports no value for 'B2' (the initial peripheral cTnI
  level), so the peripheral compartment starts empty.
* **Fr random effect.** The Methods state an exponential (log-normal) model
  for every parameter. A log-normal `Fr` exceeds 1 for about 14% of cTnI
  subjects (typical 0.53, omega 0.59), which would make the second release
  chain negative. `Fr` is therefore encoded logit-normal (`logitfslow`), the
  usual Monolix choice for a fraction, with omega on the logit scale. Chain 1
  is the slower chain for both CK and cTnI, which is why the parameter is
  named `fslow`.
* **Fixed-to-zero random effects.** omega n2 and omega ktr2 of the CK model
  were fixed to 0 and are omitted rather than carried as zero-variance etas.
* **Conditioning-arm covariate for CK-MB.** The Results say the reference
  category was "control and RIPer arms" and the other "RIPer/RIPer + IPOST".
  Because the RIPer and RIPer + IPOST arms were merged after they did not
  differ (p = 0.89), the reference is the control arm and
  `TRT_CONDITIONING = 1` covers both conditioned arms. This matches Figure 3,
  where both conditioned arms lie below control.
* **cTnI units.** Table 2 and Figure 3 label cTnI in mg/L, and Figure 2 in
  IU/L. The magnitudes (median peak 97) correspond to ug/L (ng/mL) on the
  contemporary cTnI assays. The model is linear in the biomarker level, so
  only `addSd` depends on the unit; the printed mg/L is kept.
* **Time origin.** Time is measured from each patient's first blood sample
  (before PCI), not from symptom onset or reperfusion. The models have no
  dose records; supply observation rows on `central` from time zero.
* **Covariates.** `AAR_PCT` (area at risk, % of abnormally contracting
  segments on left ventriculography) and `TRT_CONDITIONING` (conditioning arm
  versus control) are new entries in the covariate register. Both act on
  `BTOT` without centring, so the tabulated `BTOT` is the value at AAR = 0 in
  the control arm.
* **Virtual cohort.** AAR is log-normal from the Table 1 median and IQR, and
  arm sizes keep the trial ratios at no more than 200 subjects per arm.
